title: Carboplatin and paclitaxel · lung cancer
purpose: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning. For advanced lung cancer, it aims to control cancer and help symptoms. Your team confirms which aim applies to you.

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises microtubules, structures cells use during division. It can slow cancer growth but also harm healthy nerves, blood-forming cells and hair follicles. Both medicines are planned on Day 1 of each of four cycles.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse immediately about infusion symptoms. Report numbness, tingling, fever, painful muscles, mouth sores or diarrhoea.

agents.name: Carboplatin
agents.explanation: Carboplatin forms links in DNA that hinder copying and repair. Healthy tissues can also be harmed. Its dose depends on target exposure (AUC) and measured or estimated kidney function; AUC is not a fixed number of milligrams. Both medicines are planned on Day 1 of each of four cycles.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, nausea, hearing changes or numbness. Tell the nurse immediately about possible allergy during the infusion.

phases.label: Four chemotherapy cycles
phases.detail: Both medicines on Day 1, repeated every 21 days for four planned cycles, unless cancer progresses or side effects require a change. This standalone plan does not include nivolumab or radiotherapy.

phases.label: Review and next plan
phases.detail: Your team reviews recovery and the next steps. Scans or other treatments depend on the cancer setting; they are not automatically scheduled by this guide.

timeline.label: Symptoms can occur any day
timeline.text: No guaranteed safe or recovery days

day_groups.title: Treatment day
day_groups.body: Paclitaxel is given into a vein over three hours, followed by carboplatin over 30 minutes. Blood review, preparation, prevention medicines and observation make the visit longer.
day_groups.action: Tell staff immediately about flushing, rash, chest or throat tightness, breathing difficulty or feeling faint.

day_groups.title: Early days at home
day_groups.body: Follow your prescribed anti-sickness plan. Aches, nausea, tiredness and bowel changes can occur.
day_groups.action: Call if symptoms are uncontrolled or you cannot drink; fever or sudden illness needs urgent advice.

day_groups.title: Keep watching for symptoms
day_groups.body: Low blood counts can increase infection or bleeding risk. The timing varies between people.
day_groups.action: Call urgently for fever, shivering, sudden illness or unusual bleeding; do not wait for blood tests.

day_groups.title: Review before the next cycle
day_groups.body: Symptoms may improve or persist. Describe the worst symptoms since treatment, not just how you feel today.
day_groups.action: Confirm blood tests and the next appointment. Report numbness, weakness or hearing changes before treatment.

support.title: One written prevention plan
support.text: Take allergy-prevention and anti-sickness medicines exactly as prescribed. The team combines steroid instructions into one plan; do not add leftover tablets or miss a premedication without telling the team.

support.title: Drinking and symptoms
support.text: Ask for help with poor intake, vomiting, diarrhoea or reduced urine. Follow your individual fluid advice rather than a fixed target.

support.title: Practical help
support.text: Plan transport if medicines make you drowsy. Bring your medicine list, symptom record and treatment card.

questions.q: What is the aim in my case?
questions.a: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning. For advanced lung cancer, it aims to control cancer and help symptoms. Your team confirms which aim applies to you.
Both medicines on Day 1, repeated every 21 days for four planned cycles, unless cancer progresses or side effects require a change. This standalone plan does not include nivolumab or radiotherapy.

questions.q: Does this include immunotherapy or radiotherapy?
questions.a: No. If either is prescribed, ask for the matching combination plan. A four-cycle chemotherapy-only guide cannot replace the three-cycle nivolumab plan before surgery.
Your consultant agrees scan timing for your cancer and treatment aim; the NCCP regimen does not prescribe a fixed scan interval.

questions.q: Who do I ring if unwell?
questions.a: Keep the unit’s daytime and out-of-hours numbers on your treatment summary and card. Call immediately for fever or sudden illness, even between appointments.

chapters.title: Your treatment and its aim
chapters.intro: After surgery, treatment aims to reduce the chance of lung cancer returning. For advanced lung cancer, it aims to control cancer and help symptoms. Your team confirms which aim applies to you.

items.title: Which setting?
items.text: NCCP 00304 a/b: selected adjuvant or locally advanced, recurrent or metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer. These indications are off-label in Ireland and require the local consent and approval process. Nivolumab combinations use a separate guide.

items.title: Evidence and choices
items.text: The adjuvant CALGB 9633 study did not show a statistically significant survival benefit for the whole stage IB group in its mature analysis. An exploratory large-tumour subgroup suggested benefit. Advanced-disease trials support platinum-doublet activity but do not turn adjuvant results into an advanced-cancer prognosis.

items.title: Other options
items.text: Discuss suitable alternative treatments, clinical trials, symptom support and the option of not proceeding. Choices depend on stage, previous treatment and your priorities.

chapters.title: Recognising side effects
chapters.intro: Call your oncology team immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, new breathing difficulty, chest pain, unusual bleeding, severe abdominal pain or inability to drink. Report new numbness, weakness or hearing change promptly. Follow the unit’s emergency instructions and do not wait for the next visit.

items.title: Nerves and hearing
items.text: Report tingling, numbness, weakness, balance problems, ringing in the ears or hearing change early. Some effects may last after treatment.

items.title: Infusion symptoms
items.text: Tell staff immediately about flushing, rash, breathing difficulty, chest or throat tightness, or feeling faint.

items.title: Daily care
items.text: Ask for help with eating, drinking, fatigue, mouth care, hair loss or bowel symptoms. Talk about fertility, contraception and pregnancy before treatment.

evidence.title: What the evidence means
evidence.intro: The adjuvant CALGB 9633 study did not show a statistically significant survival benefit for the whole stage IB group in its mature analysis. An exploratory large-tumour subgroup suggested benefit. Advanced-disease trials support platinum-doublet activity but do not turn adjuvant results into an advanced-cancer prognosis.
evidence.summary: The adjuvant CALGB 9633 study did not show a statistically significant survival benefit for the whole stage IB group in its mature analysis. An exploratory large-tumour subgroup suggested benefit. Advanced-disease trials support platinum-doublet activity but do not turn adjuvant results into an advanced-cancer prognosis.
evidence.interpretation: Benefit depends on the cancer stage, treatment aim, fitness and alternatives. Trial averages are not a prediction for you.
evidence.caveat: The stage IB study does not establish benefit across every stage in the NCCP indication, and exploratory subgroup findings are uncertain.
